videoIdeas.title: The 3 words that calm you before you speak
videoIdeas.hook: You're not nervous because you're weak. You're nervous because you care — now let's use that.
videoIdeas.rationale: Listicle/how-to format is carrying doctordaanish ('5 careers', '5 specialties') and birdtart ('networking questions'). You have almost nothing on public speaking mechanics despite it being a core pillar. A tight, numbered 'how-to' fills that gap in a proven format.
videoIdeas.script:
You're not nervous because you're weak. You're nervous because you care — now let's use that.

Three things, before you say a word.

One. Slow your first sentence down on purpose. Everyone rushes the opener because they want it over with. The room reads speed as fear. Say your first line like you've got all the time in the world.

Two. Find one face, not the whole crowd. Your brain can't 'perform to 200 people.' It can talk to one. Pick a friendly face, talk to them, move to the next.

Three. Breathe out before you start, not in. We gulp air when we panic. Push it all out first. Empty lungs force a calm, low breath back in.

The shaking doesn't mean stop. It means you're about to do something that matters. Do it scared.

visuals.setting: Standing, mid-frame, plain wall or empty hall that reads 'about to go on stage.' Smart-casual, calm energy — you're the one who's done this a hundred times. Minimal movement, steady eye contact with lens.
visuals.visualHook: Open on a tight shot of your hands visibly shaking, then cut to your face, steady, as you say the first line. On-screen text: 'nervous = you care'
otherHookIdeas: Cold open mid-breath: a loud exhale straight into camera before any words
On-screen text punchline first: 'STOP breathing in. Do this instead.'
Pattern interrupt — walk INTO frame from the side like you just stepped off a stage

videoIdeas.title: A title is not leadership
videoIdeas.hook: Half the 'leaders' you know are just people with a title and a loud voice.
videoIdeas.rationale: You have no pure leadership content in your top posts despite it being pillar one. dinoo's critique-style posts ('red pill influenced content') and saffanabanana's blunt takes pull strong engagement. A sharp, contrarian definition piece plays to your 'older brother' voice.
videoIdeas.script:
Half the 'leaders' you know are just people with a title and a loud voice.

Real talk — a title is given. Leadership is taken, quietly, before anyone notices.

The Prophet ﷺ was leading people before there was an ummah. No title. No podium. People followed because of who he was, not what he was called.

So here's the test. Take the title away. The committee role, the 'brother in charge,' the badge. Do people still come to you? Do they still listen?

If yes — you were always a leader. If no — you were just holding a position.

Stop chasing the title. Build the thing that makes the title irrelevant.

visuals.setting: Seated or standing, direct address, slightly serious tone. Neutral background. Dress one notch sharper than usual — the visual should back up the authority of the words.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text appears word by word: 'TITLE ≠ LEADER' as you deliver the first line, unsmiling.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open with a rhetorical: hold up a lanyard/badge, then drop it out of frame
Quick-cut 'test' format — freeze on the line 'take the title away'
Direct accusation hook: point at camera on 'half the leaders you know'

videoIdeas.title: Responding to the worst advice young Muslims get
videoIdeas.hook: Someone with 2 million followers told young brothers this. It's quietly ruining them.
videoIdeas.rationale: dinoo's highest non-viral posts are react/critique of 'red pill' content misguiding the youth (24k views, 213 comments). This stitch/response format drives comments hard and sits perfectly in your blunt voice. It's a format you've never tried.
videoIdeas.script:
Someone with two million followers told young brothers this. It's quietly ruining them.

The advice? 'Never let anyone see you weak. Never apologise. Dominate every room.'

Sounds strong. It's actually fragile.

Because a man who can never be wrong, never say sorry, never ask for help — that's not strength. That's a glass ego wearing a costume.

The strongest man I know of, ﷺ, cried. Asked for counsel. Took advice from a teenager when the teenager was right.

Strength isn't never bending. It's being secure enough to bend without breaking.

Stop taking masculinity lessons from men who are clearly insecure. Take it from the one who actually had nothing to prove.

visuals.setting: Close, conversational, lower lighting — a 'let's be honest for a second' energy. You talking straight to the viewer like a side conversation.
visuals.visualHook: Split screen / on-screen text showing a fake 'influencer' quote card, then you shaking your head as the first line lands.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open mid-sentence: '...and that's the problem with that advice'
On-screen text punchline: 'this is NOT strength' over the quote
Pause-and-react: read the bad advice, hold a silent beat, then respond

videoIdeas.title: How to actually talk to people at an event
videoIdeas.hook: Stop asking 'so what do you do.' It's why nobody remembers you.
videoIdeas.rationale: birdtart's single biggest hit (979k views) is literally 'networking questions to authentically connect.' Massive proven demand. You can own this for the young Muslim audience with your directness — a clear content gap you haven't touched.
videoIdeas.script:
Stop asking 'so what do you do.' It's why nobody remembers you.

Everyone asks the same three dead questions. What do you do, where you from, you alright. Then you both stand there.

Here's what actually works.

One. 'What's been keeping you busy lately?' — not their job, their life. People light up when you ask about the thing they actually care about.

Two. 'How did you end up here?' — everyone has a story and almost nobody gets asked for it.

Three. Shut up and listen to the answer. Properly. Don't wait for your turn to talk.

Connection isn't about being interesting. It's about being interested. Get that round the right way and people will remember you long after the event ends.

visuals.setting: Film at or near an actual event space — a hall, a foyer, people-ish background if possible. Smart-casual, warm energy, slightly higher pace than the serious videos.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text crosses out 'so what do you do?' with a red line as you say it.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open walking through a crowd/event space
Punchline-first text: 'the question that makes people remember you'

videoIdeas.title: The leader who freed a people with 7,000 men
videoIdeas.hook: In 711, a man burned his own ships so his army couldn't retreat. Here's the leadership lesson nobody teaches.
videoIdeas.rationale: Your Tariq bin Ziyad historical post (437 views) outperformed most of your non-running content and sits dead centre in your niche. Reframing history as a leadership lesson — rather than just narration — gives it a clear takeaway and replay value.
videoIdeas.script:
In 711, a man burned his own ships so his army couldn't retreat. Here's the leadership lesson nobody teaches.

Tariq bin Ziyad lands in Spain. Seven thousand men against a kingdom. And the first thing he does is destroy the only way home.

People call it crazy. It wasn't crazy. It was clarity.

He understood something about people — when retreat is an option, people hold a little back. Part of them is always planning the exit. Remove the exit, and every ounce of effort goes forward.

That's leadership. Not shouting. Not a title. Creating a situation where your people have no choice but to become who they're capable of being.

You don't need ships to burn. But look at your own life — what exit are you secretly keeping open, that's quietly letting you give less than everything?

visuals.setting: More cinematic — darker, moodier lighting, serious tone, maybe a stark backdrop. This is a story piece, let the delivery slow and weighty.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text over a black screen: '711 AD' then hard cut to you mid-sentence about burning the ships.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open on the single word 'retreat' then crossing it out
Question flip ending re-used as alt hook: 'what exit are you keeping open?'
Slow push-in on your face as you deliver the opener

videoIdeas.title: In the room beats fastest in the room
videoIdeas.hook: I'm not the fastest runner out there. I stopped caring. Here's what changed.
videoIdeas.rationale: Your running post ('might not be the fastest, but I am in the room') is your single best performer — 926 views, 119 likes, 11 comments. The personal, honest, showing-up angle is clearly what your audience connects with. Lean into the format that's actually working for YOU, not just competitors.
videoIdeas.script:
I'm not the fastest runner out there. I stopped caring. Here's what changed.

For years I didn't start things because I knew I wouldn't be the best at them. Couldn't be the top speaker, so why speak. Wouldn't win the race, so why run.

That's a quietly arrogant way to live, by the way. It assumes you deserve to be good before you've earned it.

So I flipped it. Forget being the best in the room. Just be in the room. Keep turning up when you're slow, when you're bad, when you're embarrassed.

Because here's what nobody tells you — ninety percent of people never even enter the room. They talk about it from outside.

Being in the room, consistently, badly, is already ahead of almost everyone. Speed comes later. Showing up comes first.

visuals.setting: Film mid-run or straight after — slightly out of breath, real, authentic. Outdoors, natural light. This is your proven lane: raw and personal, not polished.
visuals.visualHook: Cold open mid-run, breathing hard, then you stop and turn to camera for the first line. On-screen text: 'last place. still here.'
otherHookIdeas: On-screen text punchline first: 'being bad at it is the point'
Candid post-run talking head, sweaty, no setup
Pattern interrupt: start with 'this is arrogant and nobody admits it'

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: This is your best post for a reason — 926 views, 119 likes, 11 comments. The caption is short, personal, and has a built-in reframe ('not the fastest, but I am in the room'). It's a mindset lesson disguised as a personal moment, and it's quotable. The audience clearly connects with honest, first-person showing-up content more than anything else you post.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: You left the insight sitting only in the caption. Turn the line itself into a spoken hook and a full video — people engaged with the idea, so give them more of it. Also pin this and build a mini-series around 'in the room' consistency; you found your lane, mine it.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: The Tariq bin Ziyad post pulled 437 views with a strong, specific hook ('In 711 AD, Christians were begging Muslims to liberate them'). Concrete dates and a surprising framing stop the scroll — this is history as hook, which suits your niche perfectly.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: Zero comments means it informed but didn't provoke a response. Narration alone doesn't travel — reframe it as a leadership LESSON with a direct question to the viewer at the end ('what exit are you keeping open?'). Give people a reason to reply, not just to nod.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 376 views and a relatable, funny caption ('Never running through a park at night ever again 😭'). The humour and vulnerability make you human and keep you in the same 'running/personal' world your audience already rewards. Easy, authentic, low-effort-high-relatability.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: It's pure entertainment with no takeaway, so it builds affinity but not authority. Every few of these, land a point — tie the fear or the discomfort back to a mindset lesson. Right now it's a moment; make one of them a moment with a message.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: You led with a real pain point your audience feels ('Burnout affects so many of us') and anchored it in faith-adjacent self-development. The topic is bang in your niche and the opener names the audience directly.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: 209 views, 21 likes — your lowest performer, and it reads as a product promo for the Sabr app. The algorithm and the audience both smell a plug. If you cover burnout again, teach it first as your own lesson with zero product, build trust, and mention tools only after you've given real value for free.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 289 likes — your most LIKED post. The hadith-backed call to action ('Whoever sees an injustice...') plus a clear moral stance mobilised people. Conviction and a named cause move your audience hard; this proves they'll show up for you when you take a real position.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: It was a Sidecar (carousel) with only 1 comment — high likes, low conversation, and no video reach. Your audience rewards video. Deliver this kind of principled stance as a talking-head reel so it actually travels, and end with a question or a concrete action so the energy converts into comments, not just a tap.
